metaDescription: Six pasta makers compared by extruder versus roller design, motor power, thickness settings, flour capacity and how much hand work each one leaves to you.
expertTake: The Philips 7000 Series is the pick for people who want fresh pasta from flour and water with almost no hand work, and the Marcato Atlas 150 with the Atlasmotor is the pick for cooks who want true rolled sheets. The Marcato manual machine is the classic for lasagna and filled pasta. If you make pasta twice a year, the manual machine is the better buy.
introParagraphs: A pasta maker comes in two families that do different jobs. An extruder mixes and kneads dough in a chamber and pushes it through a die to make shapes such as spaghetti and penne, while a roller thins a sheet of dough between smooth rollers and cuts it into ribbons. The first is automatic and fast, and the second gives the texture and flexibility of hand-rolled pasta.

The choice depends on the pasta you want. Long noodles and short tubes come from extruders, lasagna sheets, ravioli and fettuccine come from rollers, and a few machines do both. This guide ranks the lineup by how well each design does its job and by what you still have to do by hand, since a pasta maker that needs constant attention is not a time saver.

products.name: Philips 7000 Series Pasta Maker, ProExtrude, 8 Discs
products.description:
Philips' 7000 Series is a fully automatic extruder: you add flour and liquid, and the machine mixes, kneads and extrudes through one of eight shaping discs. The maker claims pasta in under 10 minutes and up to 8 portions in one go, and a versatile mixing function handles dough beyond pasta.

Automation is why it leads. A traditional pasta machine needs you to make the dough, knead it, rest it and feed it through rollers, while this machine takes dry flour and liquid and delivers noodles in minutes. Eight discs cover spaghetti, penne, fettuccine and other shapes, and an 8 portion capacity feeds a family. A 150 watt motor is modest, but the extrusion is slow and steady.

Extruded pasta has a different texture from rolled pasta, with a rougher surface that holds sauce well and a firmer bite. Weigh flour and liquid precisely, since extruders need a crumbly dough, not a smooth one. Brush the discs clean when dry and do not soak them. Keep spare discs for different shapes. For best results, use a high-protein flour or semolina blend, weigh the flour on a scale rather than by cup, and add liquid slowly through the opening while the machine kneads.
products.bestFor: Families who want fresh pasta shapes with almost no hand work.
pros: Fully automatic mixing, kneading and extruding
cons: Extruded texture differs from rolled pasta

products.name: Marcato Atlasmotor 110V Electric Pasta Machine, Atlas 150 and Motor

specList.label: Includes
specList.value: Atlas 150, hand crank, clamp, Pastadrive motor

products.description:
This set pairs the Italian Atlas 150 roller with a Pastadrive motor, a hand crank and a clamp, so you can roll pasta sheets up to 150 millimeters, or 6 inches, wide either by hand or electrically. An adjustment knob with ten clear positions sets the thickness, and the whole thing is made and assembled in Italy.

The motor changes the workflow. A hand-cranked roller needs two hands, one for the crank and one for the dough, and the motor frees one so you can guide the sheet. Rolled pasta has the smooth, springy texture that people associate with fresh pasta, and the machine produces lasagna sheets, fettuccine and, with attachments, other cuts.

It is more work than an extruder, since you make and rest the dough, but the result is the classic. Clamp it firmly to a counter, dust the dough lightly with flour and fold and re-roll at the widest setting before stepping down. Wipe the rollers with a dry brush and never wash them in water, which rusts them.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want true rolled sheets and a motor to help.
pros: Made in Italy with a clamp and crank
cons: You make and rest the dough yourself
Needs a counter edge for the clamp

products.name: GVODE Electric Pasta Maker, Stainless Housing, 700W, 3-in-1
products.description:
GVODE's electric roller has a stainless steel shell, two speeds with reverse, eight thickness settings from 0.4 to 2 millimeters and a 3-in-1 roller and cutter set. The listing gives 700 watts maximum power and advises running in 15 minute batches with a 5 minute cool-down.

The stainless housing is what distinguishes this model from the plastic-bodied electric rollers. It resists dents and wipes clean without staining, and the listing contrasts it with a lighter plastic version at around 8 pounds. Reverse is a useful safety feature when dough catches, and two speeds let you roll slowly for thick dough.

The run limit matters: a 700 watt maximum motor heats when it runs continuously, so follow the cool-down. Against the Marcato set, the GVODE is a one-piece electric machine at a different price tier with less brand history. Dust the dough, start thick and step down, and brush the rollers clean when dry. Keep it away from water. Because the machine is electric, set up on a stable counter, keep a bowl for trimmings and never reach near the rollers with loose sleeves or long hair. The reverse function is there to release a stuck sheet, so stop the machine before you pull dough out by hand.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want an electric roller with a stainless body and reverse.
pros: Eight thickness settings from 0.4 to 2 mm
cons: 15 minute run limit with a 5 minute rest

products.name: VEVOR Electric Pasta Maker, 150W, 8 Shapes, 4 Modes

specList.label: Kneading
specList.value: Two-way kneading rod with four-dimensional mixing

products.description:
VEVOR's extruder uses a 150 watt motor, comes with eight pasta shapes and four intelligent modes, and handles 500 grams of flour, enough for about four people. A two-way kneading rod and four-dimensional mixing are meant to mimic hand kneading, and the box includes recipes and simple ratios.

It competes directly with the Philips 7000 and costs less. The difference is polish and track record: the Philips has a long brand reputation and a stated 8 portion capacity, while the VEVOR offers similar capability with a shorter history. The four modes automate the mixing and extruding sequence, and 500 grams of flour is a sensible family batch.

Follow the recipe ratios exactly, since extruders need a crumbly dough, and add liquid slowly. Let the machine run through its mode, extrude and cut the pasta as it exits. Brush the discs clean when dry and do not soak them. For the price of a mid-range hand machine, it offers an automatic workflow.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want an automatic extruder at a lower price.
pros: 500 g flour for about four people
cons: Less brand track record than the Philips

products.name: Philips Viva Compact Pasta and Noodle Maker, 3 Discs
products.description:
The Viva is a compact Philips extruder that automatically kneads and extrudes two to three servings of fresh pasta in about 18 minutes. It ships with three shaping discs for spaghetti, penne and fettuccine, and the listing says you can vary flour and add egg, herbs or vegetable juice.

It is the small sibling of the 7000 Series, with a smaller batch, a slower cycle and fewer discs. For a couple or a small family, that is enough, and the compact body stores more easily. The automatic stirring design mixes and extrudes without your intervention.

Use the supplied cup to measure flour and liquid exactly, since extruders are fussy. Let the machine run, extrude and cut as it exits, and brush the discs clean when dry. If you want more shapes or bigger batches, the 7000 Series is the step up.
products.bestFor: Couples and small households who want a compact automatic extruder.
pros: Works with egg, herbs and vegetable juice
cons: Smaller batch of two to three servings

products.name: Marcato Atlas 150 Manual Pasta Machine, Made in Italy
products.description:
The Atlas 150 is the classic hand-cranked pasta machine: nickel and chrome-plated steel rollers and cutters with an ABS crank, making lasagna sheets, fettuccine and tagliolini. It is made in Italy and is the reference design that many electric machines copy.

Its virtue is simplicity and durability. There is no motor to fail, the rollers are precisely ground and the machine lasts for decades with simple care. It makes the same smooth, springy rolled pasta as the motorized set, and costs far less than any electric machine. You give up the motor and the automation, so you make the dough, knead it, rest it and crank each pass.

Clamp it to a counter, dust the dough with flour and pass it through at the widest setting several times before stepping down. Brush the rollers clean when dry and never wash them. It is the right machine for lasagna, ravioli sheets and special-occasion pasta, and a poor fit if you want pasta on a weeknight in ten minutes.
products.bestFor: Cooks who make rolled pasta occasionally and want a lasting tool.
pros: Precision steel rollers with no motor to fail
cons: Needs a counter edge for the clamp

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Philips 7000, Philips Viva and VEVOR are extruders, pushing dough through dies for shapes like spaghetti and penne. The Marcato machines and the GVODE are rollers, thinning dough into sheets for lasagna and fettuccine. Pick the family that makes the pasta you eat. Many households discover that they cook spaghetti and penne most often, which favors an extruder, while a cook who loves lasagna, tortellini and ravioli will be happier with a roller and a rolling pin. Think about the last five pasta dinners you cooked and let that list decide, rather than the feature count on the box.

Extruders mix and knead automatically from flour and liquid, with a recipe that takes under 20 minutes. Rollers need you to make, knead and rest the dough, then crank or run each pass. A motor helps the roller, as on the Atlasmotor, but the dough work remains. A typical roller routine is to mix flour and eggs into a shaggy dough, knead for several minutes, rest it for thirty minutes so the gluten relaxes and then roll and cut, which stretches a simple supper into an hour or more. Extruders collapse most of that into one loading step, which is the real time saving.

The Philips 7000 claims up to 8 portions, the VEVOR 500 grams of flour for about four people and the Viva two to three servings. A roller makes as much as you have dough for. Match batch size to your household. A rough guide is about 100 grams of flour per person for a main course, so 500 grams feeds about four, which matches the VEVOR's stated capacity. Fresh pasta cooks in a few minutes and does not keep well, so make only what you will eat, or dry or freeze the rest the same day.

The Atlasmotor offers ten positions, the GVODE eight from 0.4 to 2 millimeters. Fine control lets you roll thin sheets for ravioli and thicker ones for fettuccine. Extruders fix the shape by the die. Thickness in a roller affects both cook time and texture: thin sheets cook in a minute or two for ravioli and delicate noodles, while thicker ones hold up to heavy sauces and need a few minutes longer. Start at the widest setting, fold and pass the dough several times to smooth it, then step down one setting at a time rather than skipping.

The GVODE lists 700 watts maximum and a 15 minute run followed by a 5 minute rest. The extruders run at 150 watts for slow, steady work. Follow the manufacturer's duty cycle to protect the motor. A pasta machine under load is working a dense dough, and a motor that smells hot or slows down is asking for a rest. Cutting the dough into manageable pieces and rolling a few sheets at a time keeps a motorized roller inside its limits and gives you time to cut and dust as you go.

Rollers are brushed clean when dry and never washed, and extruder discs are brushed and sometimes washed per the manual. Dried dough comes off easily, and wet dough does not. Plan to let parts dry before cleaning.

maintenance.why: Dried dough crumbles off with a brush, while wet dough smears. Never soak rollers.
A dry brush removes flour without rusting steel.
Flour dust attracts moisture. A damp cloth keeps it clean.
Motors overheat when run continuously. Rest as the maker advises.

faq.q: Is an extruder better than a roller?
faq.a: It depends on the pasta you want. Extruders make shapes such as spaghetti and penne automatically from flour and liquid, with a rougher surface that holds sauce. Rollers make sheets with a smoother, more elastic texture that suits lasagna, ravioli and fettuccine, but they need dough skills and more time.

No. Water rusts steel rollers and can leave dough stuck in the gears. Let leftover dough dry for a short while, brush it off with a dry brush or a wooden pick and wipe the surfaces with a dry cloth. Never use a dishwasher, and avoid oil on the rollers, which transfers to the next batch of dough.

faq.q: Why is my extruder dough sticky?
faq.a: Too much liquid, which makes a smooth ball that clogs the die and gums the screw. Extruder dough should look like damp, pea-sized crumbs. Weigh the flour, add liquid slowly and follow the maker's ratio, adjusting by a teaspoon at a time if the dough looks dry or sticky after the first minute of mixing.

faq.q: How thin should I roll pasta?
faq.a: About 1 to 2 millimeters for fettuccine and tagliatelle, a little thicker for pappardelle, and thinner for ravioli so the filled pasta is not doughy. Test by holding the sheet up: you should be able to see the shadow of your hand through a thin ravioli sheet. Start thick and step down, since a sheet rolled too thin cannot be thickened again.

faq.q: Can I use whole wheat flour?
faq.a: Yes, but it makes a denser, nuttier pasta and needs more liquid because the bran absorbs water. Many cooks blend whole wheat with regular flour or semolina for a better texture, and let the dough rest a little longer. Extruders are fussier with whole grain, so start with a half-and-half blend and adjust the ratio from there.

faq.q: Is fresh pasta worth the effort?
faq.a: Many cooks think so for texture and flavor, since fresh pasta cooks in a few minutes and has a tender bite that dried pasta does not. An extruder reduces the effort to loading flour and liquid, while a roller turns pasta into a small project. If you cook pasta twice a month or less, a manual roller is the most economical way to try it.
